claim: Right brain injury causes visual neglect - lost awareness of left space.
source: Right brain injury causes visual neglect - lost awareness of left space.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical fact presented as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The majority of right hemisphere stroke survivors suffer acute 'neglect'.
source: The majority of right hemisphere stroke survivors suffer acute 'neglect' – lost awareness of left space (Figure 1A–C) (Buxbaum et al., 2004; Stone et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Endogenous plasticity drives neglect recovery during the sub-acute stage (<3 months post-stroke).
source: While endogenous plasticity drives neglect recovery during the sub-acute stage (<3 months post-stroke), recovery plateaus in the chronic stage (Ramsey et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramsey et al., 2016.

claim: Recovery plateaus in the chronic stage of neglect.
source: While endogenous plasticity drives neglect recovery during the sub-acute stage (<3 months post-stroke), recovery plateaus in the chronic stage (Ramsey et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramsey et al., 2016.

claim: Chronic neglect predicts poor functional outcome, entailing prolonged hospitalization, reduced independence, and lasting disability.
source: Chronic neglect predicts poor functional outcome, entailing prolonged hospitalization, reduced independence, and lasting disability (Jehkonen et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jehkonen et al., 2006.

claim: There is currently no clinically established effective treatment for chronic neglect.
source: There is currently no clinically established effective treatment (Bowen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bowen et al., 2013.

claim: Single-session experimental interventions can improve neglect transiently (minutes to hours).
source: Several single-session experimental interventions can improve neglect transiently (minutes to hours), with intensive repetition over days/weeks/months prolonging gains, but this is costly, and dose-response data are lacking (Kerkhoff and Schenk, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kerkhoff and Schenk, 2012.

claim: During prism adaptation therapy, patients adapt to a rightward optical shift by recalibrating right arm movements leftward.
source: During prism adaptation therapy, patients adapt to a rightward optical shift by recalibrating right arm movements leftward.
evidence: This describes the prism adaptation procedure used in the study.

claim: Prism adaptation can improve left neglect, but the benefit of a single session is transient (~1 day).
source: This can improve left neglect, but the benefit of a single session is transient (~1 day).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about prism adaptation therapy.

claim: Tonic disinhibition of left motor cortex during prism adaptation enhances consolidation, stabilizing both sensorimotor and cognitive prism after-effects.
source: Here we show that tonic disinhibition of left motor cortex during prism adaptation enhances consolidation, stabilizing both sensorimotor and cognitive prism after-effects.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2-7.

claim: Just 20 min of combined stimulation/adaptation caused persistent cognitive after-effects (neglect improvement) that lasted throughout follow-up (18–46 days) in three longitudinal patient case series.
source: In three longitudinal patient case series, just 20 min of combined stimulation/adaptation caused persistent cognitive after-effects (neglect improvement) that lasted throughout follow-up (18–46 days).
evidence: Supported by patient data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Adaptation without stimulation was ineffective in the three patient case series.
source: Moreover, adaptation without stimulation was ineffective.
evidence: Supported by comparison of sham vs. anodal conditions in patient data (Figure 7).

claim: Stimulation reversed treatment resistance in chronic visual neglect.
source: Thus stimulation reversed treatment resistance in chronic visual neglect.
evidence: This is an inference from the patient data showing that previously unresponsive patients improved with stimulation.

claim: M1 mediates the early consolidation of motor memories formed during adaptation.
source: We targeted M1 based on evidence that this brain region mediates the early consolidation of motor memories formed during adaptation (Hadipour-Niktarash et al., 2007; Hunter et al., 2009; Landi et al., 2011; Li et al., 2001; Richardson et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: M1 a-tDCS increases motor cortico-spinal excitability.
source: M1 a-tDCS increases motor cortico-spinal excitability (Nitsche and Paulus, 2001; Nitsche et al., 2005), lowers motor cortical inhibitory tone (Stagg et al., 2009), and strengthens synaptic efficacy of connections that are intrinsically active (Fritsch et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: M1 a-tDCS lowers motor cortical inhibitory tone.
source: M1 a-tDCS increases motor cortico-spinal excitability (Nitsche and Paulus, 2001; Nitsche et al., 2005), lowers motor cortical inhibitory tone (Stagg et al., 2009), and strengthens synaptic efficacy of connections that are intrinsically active (Fritsch et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stagg et al., 2009.

claim: M1 a-tDCS strengthens synaptic efficacy of connections that are intrinsically active.
source: M1 a-tDCS increases motor cortico-spinal excitability (Nitsche and Paulus, 2001; Nitsche et al., 2005), lowers motor cortical inhibitory tone (Stagg et al., 2009), and strengthens synaptic efficacy of connections that are intrinsically active (Fritsch et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fritsch et al., 2010.

claim: M1 a-tDCS enhances motor learning and memory formation when applied during motor tasks.
source: These physiological mechanisms, interacting with endogenous task-related brain activity, likely mediate the enhancement effects of M1 a-tDCS on motor learning and memory formation that can be observed when stimulation is applied during a range of motor tasks (Buch et al., 2017; Galea et al., 2011; Hunter et al., 2009; Panico et al., 2017; Reis et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: M1 a-tDCS increased AE magnitude during Adaptation in healthy volunteers.
source: M1 a-tDCS increased AE magnitude during Adaptation (Figure 2B, Anodal-Sham p=0.042, d = 0.5).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: M1 a-tDCS during Adaptation enhanced subsequent AE persistence during Washout and Retention in healthy volunteers.
source: M1 a-tDCS during Adaptation enhanced subsequent AE persistence during Washout and Retention (Figure 2B) (Anodal-Sham: washout p=0.008, d = 0.944; retention p=0.034, d = 0.911).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Enhanced AE persistence was a specific consequence of excitatory (not inhibitory) M1 stimulation.
source: This enhanced AE persistence was a specific consequence of excitatory (not inhibitory) M1 stimulation (Figure 2B) (Cathodal-Sham: washout p>0.4; retention p>0.8).
evidence: Supported by comparison of cathodal vs. sham conditions in Figure 2B.

claim: Enhanced AE persistence occurred with M1 a-tDCS during but not before PA.
source: Enhanced AE persistence occurred with M1 a-tDCS during but not before PA (Figure 2B versus C) (interaction: cognitive state ×tDCS: washout p=0.004; retention p=0.019).
evidence: Supported by comparison of Figures 2B and 2C showing timing-dependent effects.

claim: a-tDCS during PA applied to left posterior parietal cortex or right cerebellum had no effect on AE persistence, demonstrating anatomical specificity to M1.
source: a-tDCS during PA applied to left posterior parietal cortex (17) (Figure 2D) or right cerebellum (18) (Figure 2E) had no such effect, demonstrating anatomical specificity to M1 (Anodal-Sham Region x tDCS interaction: PPC versus M1: washout p=0.025, retention p=0.044; CB versus M1 washout p=0.027, retention p=0.033).
evidence: Supported by comparison of different brain regions in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: M1 a-tDCS had no effect on the error correction rate during Adaptation or Washout.
source: M1 a-tDCS had no effect on the error correction rate, neither during Adaptation nor Washout (Figure 2A; all p>0.9).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Neither pointing alone nor pointing during M1 a-tDCS induced a leftward bias when sham prisms were used.
source: A repeat of the protocol in Figure 2A (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) using sham prisms confirmed that neither pointing alone nor pointing during M1 a-tDCS induced a leftward bias, confirming that our key finding (Figure 2A) reflects a synergistic effect of stimulation on PA, and not an effect of a-tDCS alone.
evidence: Supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The stimulation-enhanced AE persisted across days while participants carried out their normal daily activities.
source: Hence, the stimulation-enhanced AE persisted across days while participants simply carried out their normal daily activities, indicating a robust memory trace that endured over a timescale of potential clinical relevance despite multiple changes of context.
evidence: Supported by multi-day retention data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Pointing remained significantly left-shifted in the 4 days after PA specifically in the anodal tDCS condition relative to baseline.
source: Relative to participants' mean pointing accuracy at baseline (over 4 days prior to PA), pointing remained significantly left-shifted in the 4 days after PA specifically in the anodal tDCS condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (anodal-baseline p=0.001, d = 0.73; sham-baseline p>0.5).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Across individuals, the magnitude of M1 a-tDCS-induced GABA decrease co-varied with the magnitude of AE retention increase.
source: Correlation tests confirmed our a priori one-way directional prediction of a significant positive association between the neurochemical and behavioural effects of stimulation (Figure 4) (rs (10)=−0.83, p=0.0015, 1-tail).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: When GABA decreased in response to tDCS, relative (anodal-sham) AE retention increased across individuals.
source: Across individuals, when GABA decreased in response to tDCS, relative (anodal-sham) AE retention increased.
evidence: Supported by correlation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Individuals who did not show the expected physiological response to excitatory anodal tDCS (GABA decrease) also did not show behavioural enhancement (AE retention increase).
source: Individuals who did not show this expected physiological response to excitatory anodal tDCS (i.e. disinhibition, GABA decrease) also did not show behavioural enhancement (AE retention increase).
evidence: Inferred from the correlation pattern shown in Figure 4.

claim: M1 a-tDCS-enhanced AE consolidation depends causally, at least in part, on a reduction of M1 cortical inhibitory tone.
source: In sum, this pattern of quantitative covariation between the neurochemical and behavioural effects suggests that M1 a-tDCS-enhanced AE consolidation depends causally, at least in part, on a reduction of M1 cortical inhibitory tone.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between GABA changes and behavioral changes shown in Figure 4.

claim: AE retention was significantly enhanced by M1 a-tDCS stimulation in Patient 1 with neglect.
source: Statistical analysis confirmed a significant AE was retained in both conditions. The retained AE was larger for anodal versus sham tDCS (p<0.001, d = 2.382).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of Patient 1 data shown in Figure 5.

claim: There was no response to PA + sham in the three patients with chronic neglect.
source: By contrast, there was no response to PA + sham.
evidence: Supported by comparison of sham vs. anodal conditions in patient data (Figure 7).

claim: Patient 1's neglect scores improved by ~20% absolute, ~50% relative after PA + a-tDCS in Phase A.
source: After PA + a-tDCS, Patient 1's neglect scores improved by ~20% absolute, ~50% relative (Figure 7A) (post-pre: p=0.005, d = 0.578).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of Patient 1 Phase A data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The gains observed after PA + anodal stimulation in Patient 1 Phase A were maintained for at least 88 days.
source: Rather, the gains observed after the PA + anodal stimulation session were maintained for at least a further 22 days (i.e. 88 days in total).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal data for Patient 1 shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There was a significantly greater improvement in neglect after PA + a-tDCS compared to PA + sham in Patient 1 Phase A.
source: Statistics confirmed a significantly greater improvement in neglect after PA +a tDCS compared to PA +sham (p=0.011, d = 1.52).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of anodal vs. sham conditions in Patient 1 Phase A.

claim: In Patient 1 Phase B, there was a significant and long-lasting improvement in neglect after PA + M1 a-tDCS (20% absolute, 40% relative).
source: In Phase B Patient 1 scored ~50% at baseline (Figure 7B), and just as in Phase A, there was no change in neglect after PA + sham stimulation (p>0.37). By contrast, there was once again a significant and long-lasting improvement in neglect after PA + M1 a-tDCS (20% absolute, 40% relative)(post-pre: p<0.001, d = 0.773).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of Patient 1 Phase B data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The gain from PA + M1 a-tDCS in Patient 1 Phase B was still present 46 days after the intervention.
source: This gain was still present 46 days after the intervention, the latest time-point tested.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal data for Patient 1 Phase B shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Patient 2 showed a large effect (30% absolute, 53% relative) improvement in neglect after PA + anodal stimulation.
source: Patient 2 showed a large effect (30% absolute, 53% relative; p=0.003, d = 1.836), while patient 3 showed a small effect (7% absolute, 14% relative; p=0.05, d = 0.286).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of Patient 2 data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Patient 3 showed a small effect (7% absolute, 14% relative) improvement in neglect after PA + anodal stimulation.
source: Patient 2 showed a large effect (30% absolute, 53% relative; p=0.003, d = 1.836), while patient 3 showed a small effect (7% absolute, 14% relative; p=0.05, d = 0.286).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of Patient 3 data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Group statistics combining all three patients confirmed significantly greater improvement with anodal vs. sham stimulation (p=0.005, d = 0.899).
source: Group statistics combining all three patients on Phase B absolute percent change data (Figure 7C, Figure 7—source data 1) confirmed the key prediction (Anodal >Sham: p=0.005, d = 0.899).
evidence: Supported by group statistical analysis of all three patients shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Patients exhibited 'directional hypokinesia'-like deficits with slower reach movement times when pre-cued to the left compared to the right at baseline.
source: Statistical analysis confirmed this: at baseline, despite the identical centre-out reaching movement required on every trial, patients exhibited slower movement times when pre-cued that they would have to subsequently place the ball in the left hemifield compared to the right (Left >Right, p=0.005).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of kinematic data described in Appendix 2.

claim: The hemifield difference in movement time (L > R) was abolished by prism adaptation (+ sham tDCS).
source: This hemifield difference (L > R) was abolished by prism adaptation (+ sham tDCS), which slowed movement time specifically on right-cued targets (Hemifield x Time: p=0.007).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of kinematic data described in Appendix 2.

claim: Anodal tDCS further modulated the effect of prism adaptation by speeding movement time overall.
source: Anodal tDCS further modulated this effect of prism adaptation (tDCS x Hemifield x Time: p=0.007), by speeding movement time overall (tDCS: p<0.001), with a stronger effect for right-cued targets (tDCS x Hemifield: p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of kinematic data described in Appendix 2.

claim: Stimulation-augmented PA therapy did not impair motor performance in the left hemifield.
source: Thus, stimulation-augmented PA therapy did not impair motor performance in the left hemifield.
evidence: This is an inference from the kinematic data showing no negative effects on leftward movements.

claim: The combination of PA + M1 a-tDCS improved patients' overall reaching speed.
source: Rather, the combination of PA +M1 a-tDCS (compared to sham) improved patients' overall reaching speed.
evidence: Supported by kinematic data analysis described in Appendix 2.

claim: Theoretical models of normal attention and neglect pathophysiology emphasize that right brain injury and attentional dysfunction lead to pathological hyper-excitation of the left hemisphere, causing neglect.
source: Theoretical models of normal attention and neglect pathophysiology all emphasize that right brain injury and attentional dysfunction lead to pathological hyper-excitation of the left hemisphere, causing neglect (Corbetta and Shulman, 2011; Kinsbourne, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical models in the literature.

claim: When left hemisphere activity is suppressed, neglect improves, as seen during natural recovery, secondary lesions, and inhibitory brain stimulation.
source: When left hemisphere activity is suppressed, neglect improves, as seen during natural recovery (Corbetta et al., 2005), secondary lesions (Vuilleumier et al., 1996) and inhibitory brain stimulation (Koch et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A recent study combining multi-session PA and parietal tDCS did not obtain neglect improvements of the magnitude and longevity observed in the present study.
source: A recent study aimed at such 're-balancing', by combining multi-session PA and parietal tDCS, did not obtain neglect improvements of the magnitude and longevity observed here with single-session PA + M1 a-tDCS (Làdavas et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison with prior study cited in the literature.

claim: Left M1 is an intact brain region in neglect, anatomically and functionally distinct from the direct, transcallosal and diaschitic effects of the lesion.
source: Critically, although located between hyper-excited attention structures in left parietal and frontal cortex, left M1 is an intact brain region in neglect, anatomically and functionally distinct from the direct, transcallosal and diaschitic effects of the lesion (Koch et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation and anatomical reasoning.

claim: Prior experimental work with single-session rehabilitation interventions for neglect has typically reported effects lasting <24 hr.
source: Prior experimental work with single-session rehabilitation interventions for neglect has typically reported effects lasting <24 hr (Barrett et al., 2012), contrasting markedly with the endurance of benefit observed in all three patients here (18 to 46 days).
evidence: Comparison with prior literature cited.

claim: Patient 1 responded to both M1 a-tDCS interventions (Phase A and B), and the effects accumulated.
source: Moreover, Patient 1 responded to both M1 a-tDCS interventions (Phase A and B; Figure 7A,B), and the effects accumulated, indicating that repeated interventions might further augment efficacy (for a related argument see Panico et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal data for Patient 1 shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Prism adaptation generalizes abnormally in neglect, transferring the leftward pointing bias into gains for visual cognitive deficits.
source: There is a wealth of evidence that PA generalizes abnormally in neglect, transferring the leftward pointing bias into gains for visual cognitive deficits (Jacquin-Courtois et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: All 3 patients had shown improvements in neglect after PA therapy at the sub-acute stage.
source: Importantly, all 3 patients reported here had shown improvements in neglect after PA therapy at the sub-acute stage.
evidence: Clinical history of the patients described in the study.

claim: By the chronic phase tested, the three patients were no longer responsive to prism therapy.
source: However, by the chronic phase tested here (1–1.5 years post-stroke) they were no longer responsive to prism therapy.
evidence: Clinical characterization of the patients at the time of the study.

claim: tDCS can facilitate sensorimotor function in healthy volunteers and in stroke.
source: tDCS can facilitate sensorimotor function in healthy volunteers and in stroke (Hummel et al., 2005; Zimerman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Only when stimulation has been coupled with repetitive training or skill learning have effects previously been shown to out-last a single test session.
source: However, only when stimulation has been coupled with repetitive training or skill learning have effects previously been shown to out-last a single test session (Reis et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The mechanism by which the leftward pointing bias induced by PA transfers to cognitive gains in neglect patients is not yet understood.
source: The mechanism by which the leftward pointing bias induced by PA transfers to cognitive gains in neglect patients is not yet understood (Jacquin-Courtois et al., 2013).
evidence: Acknowledgment of knowledge gap in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Lesions to parietal cortex and cerebellum have been shown to disrupt the magnitude of error correction and prism after-effects.
source: Lesions to parietal cortex (Newport et al., 2006; Pisella et al., 2004) and cerebellum (Martin et al., 1996; Weiner et al., 1983) have been shown to disrupt the magnitude of error correction and prism after-effects, but have not been shown to specifically affect consolidation.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior lesion studies.

claim: Gradual adaptation favours retention.
source: This design encouraged gradual adaptation, which itself favours retention (Michel et al., 2007), and, critically, allowed for tDCS (tonic stimulation) to be applied continuously throughout the Adaptation phase (20 min).
evidence: Supported by citation to Michel et al., 2007.

claim: Neglect patients commonly exhibit 'directional hypokinesia' - slowing of contralesionally directed (leftward) movements.
source: Since neglect patients commonly exhibit "directional hypokinesia" - slowing of contralesionally directed (i.e. leftward) movements - we expected the spatial cueing element of this task to make it sensitive to neglect.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about neglect symptoms.

claim: With the same stimulation protocol, neither healthy volunteers nor patients can reliably distinguish real from sham stimulation at 1mA.
source: With this procedure and 1mA M1 current neither healthy volunteers nor patients can reliably distinguish real from sham stimulation (Gandiga et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gandiga et al., 2006.

claim: Blinding efficacy was confirmed by post-test forced guessing (sham/real = 50:50) in healthy volunteers and in patients.
source: Blinding efficacy was confirmed by post-test forced guessing (sham/real = 50:50) in healthy volunteers (experiment shown in Figure 4) and in patients (only 1 of 4 anodal/sham pairings was guessed correctly).
evidence: Supported by blinding assessment data collected in the study.

claim: The SPECIAL sequence provides good reproducibility for measurements of GABA levels in the human brain.
source: MRS data were acquired using the SPECIAL sequence (Mekle et al., 2009), which provides good reproducibility for measurements of GABA levels in the human brain (Near et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior MRS methodology papers.

claim: Total Creatine is a commonly used reference for MRS measurements whose concentration remains relatively stable across individuals over time.
source: Estimates of neurotransmitter concentrations (GABA, Glutamate) were expressed relative to total Creatine (creatine +phosphocreatine), a commonly used reference that is easily detectable, and whose concentration remains relatively stable across individuals over time (Turner and Gant, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Turner and Gant, 2014.

claim: Stroke is a leading cause of adult disability.
source: Stroke is a leading cause of adult disability (Adamson et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adamson et al., 2004.

claim: In neglect, but not in healthy individuals, the acquired leftward bias from prism adaptation may generalize abnormally, transferring to untrained cognitive domains.
source: In neglect, but not in healthy individuals, this acquired leftward bias may also generalize abnormally, transferring to untrained cognitive domains (eg: visual search, reading, wheelchair driving), thus improving neglect (Newport and Schenk, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Newport and Schenk, 2012.

claim: Not all patients respond therapeutically to prism adaptation.
source: Here we address two key problems that limit PA's potential future transformation from an experimental intervention into an established clinical treatment (Barrett et al., 2012): (1) not all patients respond therapeutically; and (2) the benefit of a single session is transient (~1 day).
evidence: This is presented as a known limitation of PA therapy, supported by citation.

claim: The benefit of a single session of prism adaptation is transient (~1 day).
source: Here we address two key problems that limit PA's potential future transformation from an experimental intervention into an established clinical treatment (Barrett et al., 2012): (1) not all patients respond therapeutically; and (2) the benefit of a single session is transient (~1 day).
evidence: This is presented as a known limitation of PA therapy, supported by citation.

claim: A typical prism adaptation session lasts ~20 min.
source: A typical adaptation session lasts ~20 min, and induces a leftward pointing bias that persists for several minutes after prism removal - the prism 'after-effect' (AE).
evidence: This describes standard prism adaptation procedures.

claim: Prism adaptation induces a leftward pointing bias that persists for several minutes after prism removal - the prism 'after-effect'.
source: A typical adaptation session lasts ~20 min, and induces a leftward pointing bias that persists for several minutes after prism removal - the prism 'after-effect' (AE).
evidence: This describes the standard prism after-effect phenomenon.

claim: Excitation of left sensorimotor circuits, during an adaptive cognitive state, can unmask latent plastic potential that durably improves resistant visual attention deficits after brain injury.
source: Excitation of left sensorimotor circuits, during an adaptive cognitive state, can unmask latent plastic potential that durably improves resistant visual attention deficits after brain injury.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the patient data.

claim: The three patients had white matter damage overlap in the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (rIFOF), the right superior longitudinal fasciculus (rSLF) and the right anterior thalamic radiation (rATR).
source: (E) 'Disconnectome map' shows white matter damage overlap between the three patients. Red indicates white matter damage overlap in all three patients in the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (rIFOF), the right superior longitudinal fasciculus (rSLF) and the right anterior thalamic radiation (rATR).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6E with anatomical labels.

claim: The positive effects of stimulation-augmented prism therapy for visual neglect were accompanied by a motor facilitation effect on a task probe of normal everyday visually-guided reaching behaviour.
source: Hence, the positive effects of stimulation-augmented prism therapy for visual neglect were accompanied by a motor facilitation effect on a task probe of normal everyday visually-guided reaching behaviour.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the kinematic data described in Appendix 2.
